newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Belgian UCB boasts 33 percent rise in profits.
newsitem.headline: Belgian UCB boasts 33 percent rise in profits.

text.p: Belgian drugs, fine chemicals and plastic films group UCB on Wednesday reported a 33 percent increase in ordinary profit in the six months to June 30, 1997.
Ordinary profits after tax rose to 3.89 billion Belgian francs from 2.93 billion francs, but higher taxes left net profit at 4.11 billion, down slightly from 4.25 billion.
Chief executive officer Georges Jacobs insisted, however, that "what really matters are ordinary results."
He said UCB expected full year 1997 ordinary profit to rise by about 30 percent, in line with the 1996 increase.
Jacobs told a news conference that the prospects remained very favourable. "Profits should keep up with the trend that we know today...the group is in good health."
Asked whether dividends would grow at the same rate as profits in 1997, Jacobs said, "We will continue our moderate payout policy."
Asked about the recent strong rise in UCB shares on the Brussels bourse, Jacobs told Reuters after the news conference that, to his knowledge, UCB was not being taken over.
"It is strange indeed to see the value of your share multiply by three," he said, noting that 20 years ago the shares had been worth 800 francs each.
The stock took off sharply at the end of May when it was at 95,600 francs, peaking at 153,000 on July 17. It closed at 139,250 francs on Wednesday.
Analysts have said the share was overvalued at current levels, rating it at best a 'hold'.
The 33 percent increase in profits was in line with forecasts. Generale Bank predicted some downward pressure on the share on Thursday.
Jacobs noted the share was illiquid. "The market is limited, making it easier to make an impact."
At the time of the rally, market talk centred on a London broker acting on behalf of an aggressive buyer ready to pay whatever it took for UCB. But there were takeover rumours too.
Belgian bulk chemicals maker Solvay , which wants to expand more aggressvely into pharmaceuticals, was named as well as Johnson & Johnson and Pfizer , both of the U.S. Solvay denied the rumours.
Jacobs noted there was a stable core of shareholders holding 36 percent. UCB also had a poison pill structure in place since 1988, enabling it to draw up a defensive shield quickly.
"If there was a hostile threat, (core shareholders) would have over 50 percent together in two hours' time," he said.
UCB expects to launch its star anti-allergy drug Zyrtec in Japan early in 1998. Jacobs could not give a precise date.
Asked about a target for Zyrtec sales in Japan, he said, "I prefer to be very cautious. Japan is a very big market."

In the U.S. where Zyrtec has been on the market for over 20 months, sales by UCB and its partner Pfizer reached $115 million in the first half. Jacobs reiterated the sales target for Zyrtec in the U.S. for this year was "up to" $250 million.
He saw more potential for Zyrtec in the U.S. "It is a huge market of which we only have a small share...16 percent. We hope for another increase in 1998."

UCB was working on new drugs "around" Zyrtec to limit its dependence on Zyrtec. "We are confident that we will consolidate the Zyrtec position." It was making good progress on developing an epilepsy drug and a cardio-vascular drug.
